From Toys To Titans: The Rapid Evolution Of Drones
Amir Husain, Forbes, 2023-10-04

The US Army TRADOC's excellent Mad Scientist blog recently considered the question, “How big of a deal are drone swarms?” Their survey of literature and resulting conclusions were interesting. Measuring likely impact on a scale of 1-10, they rated drone swarms at a 6, which roughly translates to, “major military powers like the United States could develop counter-measures before swarms present a major risk.”

Based on the work General Allen and I did on the concept of Hyperwar in 2015, and our analysis of the combined effects of drones as a platform and distributed autonomy at scale, I consider drone swarms a significant threat and a critical capability. I think it is early to reach conclusions on how big of a threat they will be, in the fullness of time, or whether the United States will be well positioned to counter them.

Drones are an example of an integrated technology that leverages multiple underlying exponential trends of improvement. They are an "exponential technology" and have the potential of being "superexponential" because they can improve based not just on the exponential improvements in a single underlying technology of relevance, but on multiple such technologies.

What is a small drone? Batteries, a GPS sensor, a microprocessor, optional vision sensors, communications radio(s), guidance software, motors, an airframe, and a payload. Let us analyze each of these areas and consider what a small drone of the future might look like:

Battery technology is on an exponentially improving path. Not only are batteries getting cheaper, they are also getting more potent and reliable. Japanese automobile company Toyota recently announced a solid-state battery breakthrough that can recharge to capacity in just ten minutes and could extend the range of an electric vehicle to 745 miles, which is nearly double what most EVs travel today. You can now find small commercial drones for just a few hundred dollars that provide 30+ minutes of flight time. And this, while carrying a fairly high-resolution camera and lots of sensors on board. In the next 5 to 10 years one could estimate that flight times will be extended to at least an hour and a half given the expected enhancements in battery technology. A speed of 30 to 40 km an hour and a range of 120 km with a small drone that is in essence no more valuable than a few hundred dollars is astounding.

In terms of geopositioning, the United States is implementing its next-generation global position system, but even before that, the Chinese Baidu GPS will be active. This new generation of location technology not only provides precision but also an alternate system that any device can rely on if GPS signals are blocked. There's a third system, the Russian GLONASS, which is not as accurate as the new Chinese system but does provide a measure of redundancy. The new Chinese system doesn't just limit itself to providing location data but also comes with a new, global satellite-based direct messaging service that could deliver data and control messages to every system that uses this satellite infrastructure. In essence, this is a control capability unlike any we have seen before in consumer-grade, low-cost hardware. In a military context, there are plentiful means to exploit such a capability in a kinetic and information-gathering context.

Propulsion technologies are also improving quite drastically. Miniature turbines, electric motors, ducted fans, performance remote control systems, and the control mechanisms for these are more accessible now than ever before. Knowledge is openly shared on free repositories such as YouTube and many sites on the Web document the construction of hobby-grade jet-powered models that can be converted into fixed-wing, high-performance UAVs, projectiles, or loitering munitions; an increasingly popular type of “drone.”

And it’s not only that information is now so openly available, it’s also the fabrication technology. For example, 3-D printing can be used to build not just plastic parts but also components with materials such as metal. Additive manufacturing, even at the consumer level, makes the fabrication of drones relatively simple. You can even manufacture parts in “the cloud.” - or in other words, through the vast network of Chinese small-medium businesses (SMBs.) Indeed, Chinese production capacity has been brought online and is already tightly connected with individual consumers all over the world through online portals such as Alibaba and AliExpress. These sites provide access to both parts and manufacturing capacity. Their low-cost, high-performance motors and other hobbyist-grade equipment will find utility in a variety of useful military systems. Or at least, improvised systems such as those being used in large numbers in Ukraine.

Coming to sensors, we are now spoiled for choice. A massive range of sensors and communication chips are available at low prices. Infrared cameras, high capability optics, long-range reliable digital wireless links, satellite communications equipment, softwaredefined radios, magnetometers, vibration, temperature, humidity, and altitude sensors are more affordable and accurate than ever before. They can be plugged into a broad array of inexpensive compute nodes to enhance captured signals using conventional techniques such as Kalman filtering or advanced techniques involving the deep-learning powered fusion of multi-domain signals.

Twenty years ago no microcontroller and software stack was both powerful and low-cost enough to allow fully automated, long-range, high-speed flights for hobbyist-level aircraft. However, over the last 15 years, the whole scene has transformed. Sophisticated flight control software has been open-sourced and now supports a whole variety of unique airframe types. If you have a quadcopter or hexcopter, a fixed-wing aircraft, or one that’s hybrid and transitions in flight from vertical takeoff, there is likely a supported mode for it in open-source software. This means that one of the hardest parts of the job has been reduced in complexity and the set of people that can produce effective equipment including improvised unmanned combat aerial vehicles, has vastly expanded. Since the software is all open source they can plug in and begin to use it immediately while also, over time, learn by studying it. The source code is both visible and modifiable.

This is by no means an exhaustive list of capabilities now available for a small amount of money on the open international market. There is much more. And if this is the budget shopping list, imagine what a middle power can achieve if it applies national resources and talent to create an unmanned warfare capability. It turns out, we don’t have to work too hard to imagine because progress in Iran and Turkiye to name just a few places, gives us a clear indication of the direction that this line of development will take. Turkiye has made tremendous strides in developing large and small UCAVs alike, which have been deployed in multiple active theaters of combat including over Syria and Libya. These aircraft have singlehandedly been responsible for the destruction of high-quality, highvalue anti-air assets and have flown hundreds of thousands of hours seeking out and eliminating enemy targets.

Iran has not only developed a mind-bending large range of drones; everything from prop-driven medium-altitude long-endurance (MALE) aircraft like the Fotros to jet-powered bomber drones such as the Karrar to loitering kamikaze systems like the Shahed and even smaller surveillance drones. Iran was able to, at least partially, reverse engineer the technology of the captured American RQ-170 Sentinel stealth drone and proceeded to show pictures of production facilities that turn out such a design in large numbers.

Iran, in particular, is not simply producing unmanned aircraft, they're also integrating them into their doctrine and tactics. Pictures that were made public in October 2020 showed large numbers of UAVs being inducted into the military services of the country. One item on display was a UAV mounted to a small speedboat. A system of this type portends a swarm not just of boats with anti-tank guided missiles closing in to attack naval ships, but an attack that simultaneously creates a surface and aerial threat. A large swarm of these drone-equipped boats could even launch lowflying kinetic vehicles that can evade incoming fire and make a beeline for target ships, all while being launched from a stand-off distance.

Of course, nations are exploiting all the underlying technological developments we’ve covered to build better drones for themselves, and in larger numbers than ever before. But they’re also using them to export influence. As was demonstrated in the attack against Saudi Aramco's facilities, small allied groups can be provided the capability to internally assemble drones in a short time, and the supplies required to produce such drones are not particularly complex to obtain. Yet, the effect that such weapons produce can have a global impact. Easily sourced electronics, 3-D printers, and readily available software mean that countries can share designs and then trust in the expectation that the materials required to produce those designs can be locally sourced without much trouble.

At the high end, Turkiye, already the most successful drone exporter in the world, is now making the move to producing stealthy, supersonic models and will integrate air-to-air capabilities. Baykar Makina’s Akinci MALE drone integrates many onboard sensors, an air-to-air capability, and the world’s first drone-fielded supersonic ballistic missile, the UAV-230.

While drones and the mass proliferation of their enabling technologies pose a threat, they also present a massive opportunity. The rate at which these enabling technologies are developing means that counters can be shaped as quickly as threats emerge. And with superior funding and a better educational and technical base, a country like the United States is well poised to take advantage of this opportunity. The main challenge facing us is whether our defense acquisition system can operate with the speed at which technology is being developed. Because if that doesn’t change, nothing else matters.
